title: The tables go over (Matthew 21:12–13)
hook: in the temple courts he overturns the money changers' tables

segments.voice: Yesterday, hosanna: save, please, shouted for a king on a donkey. Your line was a king on a donkey. What did you lay down? Today the gentle king walks into the temple, and things get loud. Day sixty-two.

Most of us picture Jesus as gentle, and mostly he is. Children on his knee. Hands on the sick. A king on a donkey. So this scene surprises people. Picture the temple in Jerusalem the week before Passover: the holiest place in the Jewish world, and the busiest. Pilgrims have come from everywhere. The outer court, a huge open space, is full of stalls: people selling doves and animals for the sacrifices, and money changers at their tables, swapping foreign coins for the coins the temple accepted. Noise, bargaining, animals, crowds. And Jesus walks in. Today, the tables go over.
screen: `GENTLE, MOSTLY.` → `THE TEMPLE BEFORE PASSOVER.` → `STALLS, COINS AND DOVES.`

segments.voice: Matthew tells it fast, in the King James Bible: "And Jesus went into the temple of God, and cast out all them that sold and bought in the temple, and overthrew the tables of the moneychangers, and the seats of them that sold doves." Coins spilling across the stones. Birds flapping. Then he explains, quoting two prophets at once: "It is written, My house shall be called the house of prayer; but ye have made it a den of thieves." The first half is from Isaiah, and in Mark's telling the full line appears: a house of prayer for all nations. The second half is from Jeremiah, who stood in this same temple centuries earlier and warned people not to treat it as a hideout. So this isn't an attack on the temple, or on Judaism. It's a Jewish prophet in the line of Isaiah and Jeremiah, calling the temple back to what it was for. And the selling itself wasn't wicked. Pilgrims needed animals for sacrifice and the right coins for the temple tax. But this happened, many scholars think, in the outer court, the one place where people who weren't Jewish could come and pray. If that court is a market, where do they go? Make room for prayer. All four Gospels tell this story; John puts it near the start of Jesus's work, and adds a whip of cords. And look at what Matthew says happens right after the tables go over. The blind and the lame come to him in the temple, and he heals them. And children start shouting hosanna. The noise of trade gives way to the noise of healing and praise.
screen: `HE OVERTHREW THE TABLES.` · `A HOUSE OF PRAYER FOR ALL NATIONS.` · `A PROPHET LIKE JEREMIAH.` · `THEN THE BLIND AND THE LAME COME.` · then, large: `MY HOUSE SHALL BE CALLED THE HOUSE OF PRAYER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and look around the space you're in. Think of one cluttered corner in your life. It might be a real corner: a desk, a shelf, a car seat, a phone's home screen. Or a crowded hour of your day with no room left in it. Picture what that space would look like if it were clear, with room to breathe, room to think, room to pray if you pray. You don't have to clear it all right now. Just decide which one small table you'll turn over today. The bell holds the time.
The tables go over. Coins and doves scattered in the temple court, and a prophet's words: my house shall be called the house of prayer.
Your line: make room for prayer. Today, clear one cluttered corner, and leave it empty for a while. Day sixty-two.

howItsDone: Many churches read the cleansing of the temple in Lent or Holy Week. Christians often turn to it when thinking about keeping places of worship for prayer, and about money and faith.

original.note: Greek: a money changer, from kollybos, a small coin or the fee for changing money.

trapdoor: what you thought: the day Jesus lost his temper.
what it means: a prophet calls the temple back to its purpose, a house of prayer, and clears room for the blind, the lame and the children.
what a scholar hears: he quotes Isaiah 56:7 and Jeremiah 7:11 in one breath, and the trading was likely in the outer court, the one place where non-Jews could pray.

sources.quoted: And Jesus went into the temple of God, and cast out all them that sold and bought in the temple, and overthrew the tables of the moneychangers, and the seats of them that sold doves.
It is written, My house shall be called the house of prayer; but ye have made it a den of thieves.

notes: Money changers and the temple tax in Tyrian coinage; sale of sacrificial animals for pilgrims. Commonly stated; confirm.
Location in the Court of the Gentiles is a common scholarly view but not stated in the text ('many scholars think').
The script frames Jesus as a Jewish prophet in the line of Isaiah and Jeremiah and explicitly avoids framing this as an attack on Judaism. Confirm tone.
Mark 11:17 has 'of all nations'; Matthew does not. The script attributes the fuller line to Mark.
John 2:13–17 places the event early and includes the whip of cords.
